name: Urinary Problems

steps.label: Feels like
steps.question: What best describes your urinary problem?
options: Urine leaking or cannot control urination
Unable to urinate despite feeling the need

steps.label: Started
steps.question: When did you first notice this urinary problem?

steps.label: Location
steps.question: Where do you feel the discomfort?

steps.label: Duration
steps.question: How long has this urinary problem been happening?

steps.label: Each episode
steps.question: How long does each episode usually last?
steps.hint: Asked because the problem comes and goes.

steps.label: Severity
steps.question: How bothersome is this urinary problem?

steps.label: Better with
steps.question: What makes your urinary problem better?

steps.label: Worse with
steps.question: What makes your urinary problem worse?

steps.label: Other symptoms
steps.question: Do you have any other symptoms?

sources: Mohamed, Asmaa Hamdi. Health Assessment. Assistant Professor of Medical-Surgical Nursing, Ain Shams University.
Weber, J. R., & Kelley, J. H. (2014). Health Assessment in Nursing (5th ed.). Wolters Kluwer Health/Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.
Medicine LibreTexts. Pain Assessment
Cleveland Clinic. Lower Urinary Tract Symptoms (LUTS)

name: Shortness of Breath

steps.label: Feels like
steps.question: What does your breathing difficulty feel like?
options: I can’t get enough air (Air hunger)

steps.label: Started
steps.question: When did your shortness of breath begin?
options: Developed over several days to 4 weeks

steps.label: Location
steps.question: Where do you feel the discomfort related to your breathing?

steps.label: Duration
steps.question: How long does each episode of your shortness of breath last?

steps.label: Severity
steps.question: How severe is your shortness of breath? (Using the mMRC Dyspnea Scale)
options: Grade 0 - Breathless only with strenuous exercise
Grade 1 - Breathless when hurrying or walking up a slight hill
Grade 2 - Walks slower than people of the same age because of breathlessness
Grade 3 - Stops for breath after walking a short distance
Grade 4 - Too breathless to leave the house or breathless when dressing

steps.label: Better with
steps.question: What makes your shortness of breath better?

steps.label: Worse with
steps.question: What makes your shortness of breath worse?
options: Worsens when in an upright posture

steps.label: Other symptoms
steps.question: Do you experience any of these together with your shortness of breath?

sources: Nishino, T. (2011). “Dyspnoea: underlying mechanisms and treatment.” British Journal of Anaesthesia, 106(4), 463–474.
WebMD — “Dyspnea / Shortness of Breath.”
Weber & Kelley — Health Assessment in Nursing
MRC Dyspnea Scale | Primary Care Respiratory Society
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0007091217332452
https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/neuroscience/dyspnea
https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK499965/

name: Fatigue or Low Energy

steps.label: Feels like
steps.question: What does your fatigue feel like?
options: I feel tired much of the time (Tiredness)
I do not feel full of energy (Low energy)
I feel that life is empty (Emotional fatigue)

steps.label: Started
steps.question: When did the fatigue begin?

steps.label: Location
steps.question: Where is the fatigue mainly experienced?

steps.label: Duration
steps.question: How long have you been experiencing fatigue?

steps.label: Severity
steps.question: How severe is your fatigue?

steps.label: Worse with
steps.question: What makes your fatigue worse?

steps.label: Better with
steps.question: What makes your fatigue better?

steps.label: Other symptoms
steps.question: Do you experience any of the following along with your fatigue?
options: Low energy/reduced ability to do things
Changes in mood or state of mind
Feeling like you might pass out
Severe stomach, pelvic, or back pain

sources: Hardy, S. E., & Studenski, S. A. (2010). Qualities of fatigue and associated chronic conditions among older adults. Journal of Pain and Symptom Management, 39(6), 1033–1042. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jpainsymman.2009.09.026
Mayo Clinic Staff. (2026, February 20). Fatigue. Mayo Clinic.
Cleveland Clinic. (2023, April 13). Fatigue: Causes & Treatment.

name: Sleep Difficulties

steps.label: Feels like
steps.question: What kind of sleep difficulty are you experiencing?
options: Difficulty going back to sleep after waking

steps.label: Started
steps.question: When did you first notice your sleep difficulty?

steps.label: When it occurs
steps.question: When during your sleep period do you experience the most difficulty?

steps.label: Duration
steps.question: How long have you been experiencing sleep difficulties?

steps.label: Severity
steps.question: How severe is your sleep difficulty?

steps.label: Worse with
steps.question: What seems to make your sleep difficulty worse?

steps.label: Better with
steps.question: What seems to make your sleep difficulty better?

steps.label: Other symptoms
steps.question: What other symptoms do you experience along with your sleep difficulty?
options: Leg discomfort or urge to move the legs

sources: https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/11429-sleep-disorders
https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/sleep-disorders/symptoms-causes/syc-20354018

name: Vision Difficulties

steps.label: Feels like
steps.question: What kind of vision difficulty are you experiencing?
options: Difficulty seeing objects to the side
Difficulty seeing in dim light or at night
Difficulty seeing differences between objects and their background
Sensitivity to bright light or glare

steps.label: Started
steps.question: When did you first notice your vision difficulty?

steps.label: Location
steps.question: Where did you notice the vision difficulty?

steps.label: Duration
steps.question: How long have you been experiencing this vision difficulty?

steps.label: Severity
steps.question: How much does your vision difficulty affect your daily activities?
options: Prevents me from doing my usual activities

steps.label: Worse when
steps.question: When does your vision difficulty become worse?

steps.label: Better when
steps.question: When does your vision difficulty become better?
options: With glasses or prescribed visual aids

steps.label: Other symptoms
steps.question: What other symptoms or difficulties do you experience along with your vision problem?

sources: https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/blindness-and-visual-impairment
https://www.aoa.org/healthy-eyes/caring-for-your-eyes/low-vision-and-vision-rehab
https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/24446-blindness

name: Hearing Difficulties

steps.label: Feels like
steps.question: What best describes your hearing problem?
options: Difficulty hearing in noisy places or groups
Needing the TV or radio louder than others do
Ringing or buzzing in the ears (tinnitus)
Fluid or discharge from the ear
Sounds seem too loud or uncomfortable

steps.label: Started
steps.question: When did you first notice this hearing problem?

steps.label: Which ear
steps.question: Which ear is affected?

steps.label: Duration
steps.question: How long does the problem last?

steps.label: Severity
steps.question: How bothersome is this hearing problem?
steps.hint: How much does it limit conversations, phone calls, TV, or social activities?

steps.label: Better with
steps.question: What makes your hearing problem better?
options: Using a hearing aid or amplifier

steps.label: Worse with
steps.question: What makes your hearing problem worse?

steps.label: Other symptoms
steps.question: Do you have any other symptoms?
options: Avoiding social activities or feeling embarrassed

followUp: Hearing Handicap Inventory for the Elderly – Screening (HHIE-S), whispered voice test, then audiometry if positive.
sources: Bagai, A., Thavendiranathan, P., et al. (2006). Does this patient have hearing impairment? JAMA. https://www.ovid.com/journals/jama/fulltext/00005407-200601250-00025~does-this-patient-have-hearing-impairment

Identifying hearing loss and audiological rehabilitation candidacy through self-perceived hearing handicap using the Croatian version of the HHIE-S (HHIE-S-CRO). (2025). Audiology Research, 15(5). https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC12452682/
Sensitivity and specificity of hearing tests for screening hearing loss in older adults. PMC (PMC9937813). https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9937813/
Framework: Weber, J. R., & Kelley, J. H. Health Assessment in Nursing. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins. (COLDSPA)

name: Mobility Difficulties

steps.label: Feels like
steps.question: What best describes your mobility problem?
options: Difficulty standing up from a chair or bed
Needing a cane, walker, or someone's help
Difficulty with bathing, dressing, or toileting
Tiredness or shortness of breath when walking

steps.label: Started
steps.question: When did you first notice this mobility problem?

steps.label: How it started
steps.question: Did it start suddenly or gradually? Did it follow a fall, illness, or surgery?

steps.label: Location
steps.question: Where do you feel the difficulty?
steps.hint: Asked because you have pain, stiffness, or weakness in a body part.

steps.label: Duration
steps.question: How long does the difficulty last?
options: Morning stiffness lasting less than 30 minutes
Morning stiffness lasting more than 30 minutes

steps.label: Severity
steps.question: How bothersome is this mobility problem?

steps.label: Help needed
steps.question: How much help do you need to move around?

steps.label: Better with
steps.question: What makes your mobility problem better?

steps.label: Worse with
steps.question: What makes your mobility problem worse?
options: Sitting or lying for a long time

steps.label: Other symptoms
steps.question: Do you have any other symptoms?
options: Numbness or tingling in the feet
Low mood or loss of interest

followUp: Timed Up and Go (TUG), 30-second chair stand, 4-stage balance test, Katz ADL, Lawton IADL.
sources: Is the Timed Up and Go test a useful predictor of risk of falls in community dwelling older adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis. (2014). BMC Geriatrics, 14, 14. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3924230

Discriminative ability and predictive validity of the Timed Up and Go test in identifying older people who fall: systematic review and meta-analysis. (2013). Journal of the American Geriatrics Society, 61(2), 202-208.
Browne, W., & Nair, B. R. (2019). The Timed Up and Go test. Medical Journal of Australia, 210(1). https://www.mja.com.au/journal/2019/210/1/timed-and-go-test
Framework: Weber, J. R., & Kelley, J. H. Health Assessment in Nursing. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins. (COLDSPA)

name: Falls or Tripping

steps.label: Feels like
steps.question: What best describes your fall or tripping problem?
options: Felt dizzy or faint before falling
Found myself on the floor and don't remember falling
Feeling unsteady when standing or walking

steps.label: Most recent fall
steps.question: When was your most recent fall or trip?

steps.label: Falls in past year
steps.question: How many times have you fallen in the past year?

steps.label: Where it happened
steps.question: Where did you fall?

steps.label: Where hurt
steps.question: Where were you hurt?

steps.label: Duration
steps.question: How long has the falling or tripping been happening?

steps.label: Time to get up
steps.question: After the fall, how long did it take to get up?
options: Stayed on the floor for a long time

steps.label: Severity
steps.question: How bothersome is this problem or your worry about falling?

steps.label: Injury
steps.question: What was the injury?

steps.label: Better with
steps.question: What makes your falls or tripping better?
options: Sitting down to dress or bathe

steps.label: Worse with
steps.question: What makes your falls or tripping worse?
options: Poor lighting or walking at night

steps.label: Other symptoms
steps.question: Do you have any other symptoms?

followUp: CDC STEADI three key questions (fallen in the past year? feel unsteady when standing or walking? worry about falling?), then Timed Up and Go, 30-second chair stand, 4-stage balance test, orthostatic blood pressure, and medication review.
sources: Operationalization and validation of the Stopping Elderly Accidents, Deaths, and Injuries (STEADI) fall risk algorithm in a nationally representative sample. (2017). CDC Stacks. https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/50545
Mielenz, T. J., & Strogatz, D. (2020). Evaluating a two-level vs. three-level Quick-STEADI fall risk screening algorithm. Frontiers in Public Health.

Is the Timed Up and Go test a useful predictor of risk of falls in community dwelling older adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis. (2014). BMC Geriatrics, 14, 14. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3924230
Framework: Weber, J. R., & Kelley, J. H. Health Assessment in Nursing. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins. (COLDSPA)

name: Loss of Interest or Enjoyment

steps.label: Feels like
steps.question: What best describes your loss of interest or enjoyment?
options: Feeling bored most of the time

steps.label: Started
steps.question: When did you first notice this loss of interest?

steps.label: What happened then
steps.question: Did anything happen around that time (loss, illness, move, stress)?

steps.label: Duration
steps.question: Over the last 2 weeks, how often have you had little interest or pleasure in doing things?

steps.label: Severity
steps.question: How bothersome is this loss of interest?
steps.hint: How much does it affect your daily life, relationships, or self-care?

steps.label: Better with
steps.question: What makes your loss of interest better?

steps.label: Worse with
steps.question: What makes your loss of interest worse?

steps.label: Other symptoms
steps.question: Do you have any other symptoms?
options: Thoughts of death or hurting yourself (ask directly)

followUp: PHQ-2 (item 1: little interest or pleasure in doing things). If positive, use PHQ-9 or Geriatric Depression Scale (GDS-15). The GDS-15 has no suicide question, so ask about suicide risk separately.
sources: Salis et al. (2026). Validation of the Patient Health Questionnaire-2 (PHQ-2) in detecting depression among older adults. https://iris.unica.it/handle/11584/488706

Levis, B., et al. (2020). Accuracy of the PHQ-2 alone and in combination with the PHQ-9 for screening to detect major depression: systematic review and meta-analysis. JAMA. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7284301
Park, S.-H., & Kwak, M.-J. (2021). Performance of the Geriatric Depression Scale-15 with older adults aged over 65 years: An updated review 2000-2019. Clinical Gerontologist, 44(2), 83-96.
Framework: Weber, J. R., & Kelley, J. H. Health Assessment in Nursing. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins. (COLDSPA)

name: Sadness or Low Mood

steps.label: Feels like
steps.question: What best describes your low mood?

steps.label: Started
steps.question: When did you first notice this low mood?

steps.label: What happened then
steps.question: Did anything happen around that time (loss, illness, move, stress)?

steps.label: Duration
steps.question: Over the last 2 weeks, how often have you felt down, depressed, or hopeless?

steps.label: Severity
steps.question: How bothersome is this low mood?
steps.hint: How much does it affect your daily life, sleep, eating, or relationships?

steps.label: Better with
steps.question: What makes your low mood better?

steps.label: Worse with
steps.question: What makes your low mood worse?

steps.label: Other symptoms
steps.question: Do you have any other symptoms?
options: Thoughts of death or hurting yourself (ask directly)

followUp: PHQ-2 (item 2: feeling down, depressed, or hopeless). If positive (score of 3 or more is the usual cutoff; 2 or more catches more cases but gives more false positives), use PHQ-9 or GDS-15.
sources: Manea, L., et al. (2016). Identifying depression with the PHQ-2: A diagnostic meta-analysis. Journal of Affective Disorders, 203, 382-395. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27371907/

Levis, B., et al. (2020). Accuracy of the PHQ-2 alone and in combination with the PHQ-9 for screening to detect major depression: systematic review and meta-analysis. JAMA. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7284301

Accuracy in detecting major depressive episodes in older adults using the Swedish versions of the GDS-15 and PHQ-9. Upsala Journal of Medical Sciences. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC8559588/
Framework: Weber, J. R., & Kelley, J. H. Health Assessment in Nursing. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins. (COLDSPA)

name: Appetite Changes

steps.label: Appetite change
steps.question: What change have you noticed in your appetite?
steps.hint: Choose the option that best describes how you have been feeling.

steps.label: Duration
steps.question: How long have you noticed this change?
steps.hint: Choose the option that best describes the duration.

steps.label: Frequency
steps.question: How often does this happen?
steps.hint: Choose the option that best fits your experience.

steps.label: Degree of change
steps.question: How much has your appetite changed?
steps.hint: Select the option that best describes the change.
options: Unable to eat or much hungrier than usual

steps.label: Pattern
steps.question: When do you notice the change?

steps.label: Associated symptoms
steps.question: Have you noticed anything else along with this change?

steps.label: Factors affecting appetite
steps.question: What makes the appetite change better or worse?

sources: de Souto Barreto, P., et al. (2023). Assessment and management of appetite loss in older adults: An ICFSR task force report. The Journal of Frailty & Aging, 12(1), 1–6. https://doi.org/10.14283/jfa.2022.64
Healthdirect Australia. (2025). Changes to your appetite. https://www.healthdirect.gov.au/symptoms/changes-to-your-appetite

name: Anxiety or Excessive Worrying

steps.label: Experiencing
steps.question: What have you been experiencing lately?
options: Feeling on edge or unable to relax
No noticeable anxiety or excessive worrying

steps.label: When it started
steps.question: When did you first notice these feelings?

steps.label: Frequency
steps.question: How often do you feel anxious or excessively worried?
options: On and off throughout the day

steps.label: Difficulty controlling worries
steps.question: How difficult is it to control your worrying?

steps.label: Possible triggers
steps.question: What situations or concerns seem to trigger your anxiety or worrying?

steps.label: Other symptoms
steps.question: What other symptoms do you experience when you feel anxious or worried?

steps.label: Effect on daily activities
steps.question: How much does your anxiety or worrying affect your daily activities?
options: Prevents me from doing usual activities

steps.label: Helpful coping strategies
steps.question: What helps you feel less anxious or worried?
options: Spending time in a quiet environment
Seeking help from a healthcare professional

sources: Ruscio, A. M., et al. (2024). The case for eliminating excessive worry as a requirement for generalized anxiety disorder: a cross-national investigation. Psychological Medicine, 54(12), 3447–3458. https://doi.org/10.1017/S003329172400182X

Fortea, L., Solanes, A., Pomarol-Clotet, E., et al. (2025). Coping behaviors to reduce anxiety and depressive symptoms: A prospective repeated assessment study. Spanish Journal of Psychiatry and Mental Health, 18(1), 42–50. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.sjpmh.2024.08.003

name: Irritability

steps.label: Changes noticed
steps.question: What changes in mood or behavior have you noticed recently?
options: Becoming angry more easily than usual

steps.label: When it started
steps.question: When did you first notice these changes?

steps.label: Frequency
steps.question: How often do you feel irritated or frustrated?
options: On and off throughout the day

steps.label: Intensity
steps.question: How intense is your irritability when it occurs?
options: Moderate: It is difficult to stay calm
Severe: I have difficulty controlling my reactions
Very severe: It significantly affects my interactions with others

steps.label: Possible triggers
steps.question: What situations seem to trigger your irritability?
options: Feeling misunderstood or having difficulty communicating

steps.label: Other symptoms
steps.question: Have you noticed any other symptoms along with irritability?
options: Feeling sad or having little interest in activities

steps.label: Effect on daily life
steps.question: How much does irritability affect your daily activities or relationships?
options: Slightly affects my activities or interactions
Moderately affects my activities or relationships
Greatly affects my activities or relationships
Causes difficulty managing usual activities or interacting with others

steps.label: Helpful coping strategies
steps.question: What helps you feel calmer when you become irritated?
options: Spending time in a quiet environment
Talking with family or a trusted person
Taking a break from the situation

sources: Rivas-Vazquez, R. A., Rey, G. J., Rivas-Vazquez, E. V., Diaz, S. G., & Rodriguez, C. (2025). Importance of screening for irritability when assessing for geriatric depression. The Primary Care Companion for CNS Disorders, 27(1), 24m03808. https://doi.org/10.4088/PCC.24m03808

Cho, E., Hwang, S., Yang, M., Kim, E., Cho, J., & Park, C. (2026). Dynamic relationship between sleep patterns and behavioral and psychological symptoms of dementia: Longitudinal observational study. JMIR Aging, 9, e80422. https://doi.org/10.2196/80422

name: Difficulty Concentrating

steps.label: Difficulties
steps.question: What difficulties with concentration have you noticed recently?
options: Losing track of what I am doing

steps.label: When it started
steps.question: When did you first notice these difficulties?

steps.label: Frequency
steps.question: How often do you experience difficulty concentrating?
options: On and off throughout the day

steps.label: Duration of focus
steps.question: How long can you usually concentrate on a task before losing focus?
options: It varies depending on the task

steps.label: Possible contributing factors
steps.question: What seems to affect your ability to concentrate?

steps.label: Other symptoms
steps.question: Have you noticed any other difficulties along with poor concentration?

steps.label: Effect on daily activities
steps.question: How much does difficulty concentrating affect your daily activities?
options: Prevents me from completing usual activities

steps.label: Helpful strategies

Look who is complaining: Psychological factors predicting subjective cognitive complaints in a large community sample of older adults. Applied Neuropsychology: Adult, 31(3), 203–217. https://doi.org/10.1080/23279095.2021.2007387

name: Memory Difficulties

steps.label: Difficulties
steps.question: What memory difficulties have you noticed recently?
options: Repeating the same questions or stories

steps.label: When it started
steps.question: When did you first notice these memory difficulties?

steps.label: Frequency
steps.question: How often do you experience these memory difficulties?

steps.label: Changes over time
steps.question: Have your memory difficulties changed over time?

steps.label: Other difficulties
steps.question: What other difficulties have you noticed along with memory problems?
